rationale: The core leg (change in non-cash working capital scaled by assets, signed negative) is essentially Sloan's balance-sheet accrual anomaly, and multiplying by a strictly positive [0,1] stability rank only rescales magnitudes without changing the accrual ordering much, so the incremental content over a plain accrual sort is thin and largely a known interaction (accruals × earnings volatility).

The cash-flow-statement sign convention is handled correctly and the double-rank product genuinely isolates the high-buildup/unstable-margin corner, but because both legs are non-negative ranks the short leg is well defined while the long leg pools everything else, so the effective spread may be a one-sided accrual bet rather than a true interaction.

This is the accrual anomaly with the deflator swapped from assets to smoothed gross profit — a cosmetic rescaling rather than a cross-theme mechanism — and the denominator can be small or negative for low-margin and loss-making firms, which flips the ratio's sign in exactly the distressed cases the hypothesis cares about.

Using the change in taxes payable as an external validator of reported profitability improvement is an economically distinct channel from working-capital accruals and is internally consistent with the positive expected sign, though it overlaps the published book-tax-difference literature and taxes payable is a lumpy, sparsely populated item that should be checked in the coverage diagnostic.

Cumulating five years of receivable/inventory buildup is close in spirit to the net-operating-assets anomaly, and both legs load on the same underlying profitability record so the rank difference risks cancelling rather than isolating quality, but the long-horizon accumulation framing plus the RE-trend pairing is different enough (and coverage-costly enough) to be worth one test.

Multiplying two signed variables makes the top of the sort a mixture of low-accrual/improving-profit firms and high-accrual/deteriorating-profit firms, and predicting positive abnormal returns for the latter contradicts the standard (and empirically robust) reading that high accruals plus falling profitability is the worst-quality quadrant, so the expected sign is likely at odds with what the expression computes.
